elements.id-string-28: Soon after the advent of the theory of General Relativity (GR) \cite{Einstein:1915ca,Einstein:1915by}, its first exact solution, the Schwarzschild spacetime \cite{Schwarzschild:1916uq}, was discovered.
elements.id-string-29: This spacetime is commonly represented in coordinates adapted to distant static observers, which are not extendable across the event horizon.
elements.id-string-30: The complete analytic extension of the Schwarzschild metric was achieved by utilising null geodesic coordinates, a task that took over 40 years to accomplish \cite{Kruskal:1959vx}.
elements.id-string-31: The Schwarzschild geometry comprises of four regions: the Schwarzschild black hole, the Schwarzschild white hole, the Schwarzschild patch, and its mirror spacetime.
elements.id-string-32: By utilising isotropic coordinates, it was discovered that the last two regions are connected through the Einstein-Rosen bridge \cite{Einstein:1935tc}, which, although not traversable, laid the foundation for the conjecture and exploration of the theoretical and experimental existence of wormholes.

elements.id-string-34: This requires the presence of matter around the throat that violates standard energy conditions.

elements.id-string-36: The study of wormholes has greatly benefited from the initial guidelines provided by Morris and Thorne \cite{Morris:1988cz}.
elements.id-string-37: They have characterised the geometric features that a given spherically symmetric spacetime should exhibit to represent a wormhole and the energy conditions that the corresponding source should meet for the throat to be traversable.
elements.id-string-38: In recent decades, the study of wormholes has received substantial attention, not only at a theoretical level but also in the field of astrophysics.

elements.id-string-53: In this paper, we propose a novel methodology for constructing exact rotating wormholes as a means of evaluating their dynamical stability, in line with the recent results of \cite{Azad:2023iju}.
elements.id-string-54: In contrast to the Teo ansatz \cite{Teo:1998dp}, where rotation is given by the angular momentum of a rotating source, we propose introducing rotation to a static wormhole through two distinct mechanisms.
elements.id-string-55: Firstly, we consider embedding a static uncharged wormhole geometry within a rotating background spacetime, known as swirling geometry \cite{Astorino:2022aam}, which possesses characteristics similar to those of a Kerr-like rotating metric.
elements.id-string-56: Consequently, the embedded geometry rotates via a dragging effect due to the rotating background.
elements.id-string-57: On the other hand, we propose embedding a charged static wormhole in a Melvin Universe \cite{Ernst:1976mzr}, in which the rotation is acquired through the interaction of the wormhole's charge with the external magnetic field.
elements.id-string-58: To carry out these embeddings, we will utilise the Ernst scheme for electro-vacuum \cite{Ernst:1967wx,Ernst:1967by}, which allows us to identify and use a set of Lie point symmetries of the Einstein-Maxwell system known as Ehlers transformations \cite{Ehlers:1957zz,Harrison:1968}.
elements.id-string-59: These symmetries can convert a given stationary axially symmetric solution of the Einstein-Maxwell equations into a new, non-equivalent solution, providing us with a powerful solution-generating technique to explore new solutions of the Einstein-Maxwell field equations.
elements.id-string-60: We will also elaborate on how the original Ernst setup can be extended to Einstein-Maxwell-scalar theories \cite{Astorino:2013xc} and how this expands the possibility of considering wormhole geometries as seeds.

elements.id-string-422: In this study, we have developed a novel and computationally efficient methodology for constructing exact rotating wormhole configurations.
elements.id-string-423: Our approach is based on the insightful description of axially symmetric and stationary spacetimes provided by Ernst, which reveals a set of otherwise hidden Lie point symmetries in Einstein-Maxwell theory.
elements.id-string-424: These symmetries can be wisely utilized as a solution generating technique.
elements.id-string-425: Specifically, we have employed magnetic Ehlers and Harrison transformations to introduce rotation into the static Barcel\'o-Visser wormhole, a static wormhole geometry structure within the Einstein-conformal-scalar system.
elements.id-string-426: It has been demonstrated that Ehlers symmetries permit the inclusion of a minimally coupled scalar field \cite{Astorino:2013xc} , thus expanding the spectrum of solutions within the Einstein-conformal-scalar framework through the combination of these symmetries with Bekenstein transformations \cite{Bekenstein:1974sf}.
elements.id-string-427: Initially, we embarked on constructing a rotating wormhole devoid of charge by incorporating the static Barcel\'o-Visser geometry into a swirling/rotating background.
elements.id-string-428: Recent investigations have shed light on the magnetic Ehlers transformations as an efficient technique for embedding a given seed spacetime within a rotating background \cite{Astorino:2022aam}.
elements.id-string-429: It is worth noting that the rotation, although bearing resemblances to standard rotating solutions in GR, does not adhere to the Kerr type, meaning it does not arise from a rotating source but rather from a rotating background that imparts its motion onto the source.
elements.id-string-430: On the other hand, we extended the Barcel\'o-Visser wormhole to include rotation by placing its electrically charged counterpart \cite{Barrientos:2022avi} within an external magnetic field.
elements.id-string-431: This was achieved by utilizing the well-studied magnetic Harrison transformation.
elements.id-string-432: The rotational nature of the resulting solution arises from the interaction between the wormhole's electric charge and the external magnetic field present in the background.
elements.id-string-433: For both solutions, we explored various aspects including the location of the wormhole throats, traversability properties, Euclidean embeddings, asymptotic behavior, as well as the features and geometric structures of the corresponding backgrounds and ergospheres.

elements.id-string-435: Our solutions open up numerous avenues to delve into the multifaceted realm of wormhole physics.
elements.id-string-436: As previously emphasized, a significant challenge lies in studying the stability of these configurations.
elements.id-string-437: Recently, it has been demonstrated that for the class of four-dimensional wormholes within the Ellis-Bronnikov family \cite{Ellis:1973yv,Bronnikov:1973fh}, the unstable mode present in the static geometry becomes progressively more stable under increasing rotation within a perturbative regime \cite{Azad:2023iju}.
elements.id-string-438: At the second order in rotation, the emergence of a second mode has been observed, which tends to intertwine with the original unstable mode.
elements.id-string-439: It has been conjectured that rapidly rotating wormholes could attain stability.
elements.id-string-440: Therefore, our geometries provide exact, fully rotating wormhole spacetimes that can be utilized to test these stability analyses.
